videoIdeas.title: 3 things that make you look nervous when you speak
videoIdeas.hook: You're not bad at public speaking. You just do three things that make you look terrified.
videoIdeas.rationale: The listicle format is doing numbers for @doctordaanish ('5 careers I don't want' at 161k). You have almost no public speaking content live despite it being a core pillar — this fills the gap with a format that's proven right now.
videoIdeas.script: You're not bad at public speaking. You just do three things that make you look terrified. One: you speak faster the more scared you get. Slow down. Silence feels like forever to you and like confidence to everyone watching. Two: you look for the one person who isn't nodding. Stop. There's always one. He's not your audience, he's your anxiety wearing a face. Three: you apologise before you've even said anything. 'Sorry, I'm a bit nervous.' Nobody knew until you told them. Now they're watching for it. Fix those three and you don't need to be the most talented person in the room. You just need to stop handing people reasons to doubt you.

visuals.setting: Standing, mid-shot, plain wall or in an actual room with chairs behind you. Smart casual — shirt, no jacket. Calm, controlled energy, not hyped.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text '3 things that make you look nervous' while you hold up three fingers and drop one each point.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-sentence speaking too fast, then hard cut to you slow and calm
On-screen text punchline: 'Nobody knew you were nervous until you told them'
Pattern interrupt — start facing away from camera, turn to face it on the first line

videoIdeas.title: 5 things weak leaders do that they think make them strong
videoIdeas.hook: Weak leaders all do the same five things. And every one of them thinks it makes them look strong.
videoIdeas.rationale: Direct riff on the listicle format crushing it for @doctordaanish, applied to your leadership pillar — which is barely represented in your top posts. 'Weak leaders' framing gives it a saveable, controversial edge like @birdtart01's best performers.
videoIdeas.script: Weak leaders all do the same five things, and every one thinks it makes them look strong. One: they take the credit and share the blame. Should be the other way round. Two: they talk the most in every meeting. Leadership isn't volume. Three: they surround themselves with people who agree with them, then call it loyalty. It's not. It's an echo. Four: they punish honesty. Someone tells them the truth once, gets humiliated, and now nobody tells them anything. Five: they confuse being feared with being respected. Fear gets you compliance. Respect gets you people who'll still show up when it's hard. If you read those and felt something — good. That's the one to work on.

visuals.setting: Seated or standing, clean indoor setting, direct eye contact with camera. Measured, older-brother tone — not shouting. Darker palette, serious.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen counter 1–5 appearing as you speak, with the final line 'the one you felt' highlighted.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on line 5 (fear vs respect), then cut back to '5 things weak leaders do'
On-screen text: 'number 3 is the one nobody admits to'
Quick jump cuts between each number to keep pace high

videoIdeas.title: 'I'm in the room' — the standard nobody tells you about
videoIdeas.hook: I'm not the fastest runner in the room. I stopped caring about that years ago. Here's what I care about instead.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your single best post ('Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' — 866 views) proves this line resonates with your audience. Expand that exact idea into a full mindset piece while the sentiment is clearly landing.
videoIdeas.script: I'm not the fastest runner in the room. I stopped caring about that years ago. Here's what I care about instead: being in the room at all. Everyone's obsessed with being the best. Best in the gym, best in the class, best in the deen. And because they can't be the best today, they don't start. So they're not in the room. They're at home, waiting to be good enough to show up. You don't get good and then enter. You enter, and then you get good. Being the slowest person who actually turned up beats being the fastest person who only exists in their own head. Show up unqualified. Earn the right to be there by being there.

visuals.setting: Film mid-run or right after — breathless, real, outdoors. Or walking. Authentic over polished. This ties directly to your running content that already performs.
visuals.visualHook: Open on you clearly at the back of a group / last across a line, with on-screen text 'last place'.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open breathing hard post-run before you say a word
On-screen text punchline: 'You enter, then you get good — not the other way round'
Contrast cut: empty room vs you walking into it

videoIdeas.title: How they persuade you in 7 seconds
videoIdeas.hook: You think you decide what you believe. You don't. Let me show you how you get moved without noticing.
videoIdeas.rationale: @saffanabanana's whiteboard 'media literacy / brainwashing' video hit 29k and her persuasion angle is working across posts. Reframe persuasion as a public speaking skill — how it's done to you, so you can spot it and use it ethically. Fresh angle, proven subject.
videoIdeas.script: You think you decide what you believe. You don't, not always. Let me show you how you get moved without noticing. First, repetition. Say something three times in a video and your brain starts treating it as true just from familiarity. Second, confidence. We trust tone over facts. A confident wrong answer beats a nervous correct one almost every time. Third, the enemy. Give people someone to be against and they'll follow you anywhere. Now — I'm not teaching you to manipulate. I'm telling you this because it's being done to you daily, by people who don't have your interests at heart. Learn the mechanics. Then decide for yourself.

visuals.setting: Whiteboard or writing on glass, or clean talking-head with bold on-screen keywords. Analytical, calm, almost lecturing — the sharp older brother explaining how the trick works.
visuals.visualHook: Write the word 'REPETITION' big on a whiteboard before you speak, then turn to camera.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open: 'A confident wrong answer beats a nervous right one' as text on screen
Pattern interrupt — snap your fingers on 'in 7 seconds'
Underline each tactic on screen as you name it

videoIdeas.title: The lie young Muslim men keep getting sold
videoIdeas.hook: There's a version of 'manhood' being sold to young Muslim men right now and it's making you weaker, not stronger.
videoIdeas.rationale: @lifeofdinoo_ got 53k calling out red-pill influencers 'misguiding the youth.' This is a live, high-engagement conversation in your exact niche. You have the voice to do it without sounding preachy — blunt older brother, not a lecture.
videoIdeas.script: There's a version of manhood being sold to young Muslim men right now, and it's making you weaker, not stronger. It tells you to be cold. To never apologise. To see every woman as a test and every soft moment as a weakness. They dress it up as strength. It's not. It's fear with a gym membership. Real strength is boring. It's being consistent when no one's watching. It's controlling your anger instead of performing it. The Prophet ﷺ was the strongest man in any room he walked into, and he was gentle. Not weak. Gentle. There's a difference, and the guys selling you 'alpha' content have never understood it. Don't outsource your character to someone whose whole personality is a camera.

visuals.setting: Direct, serious talking-head, plain background. Lower energy, heavier tone — this one lands through conviction not hype. Darker clothing, steady frame.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'fear with a gym membership' appears over a hard cut to your face.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on the line 'Real strength is boring'
Pattern interrupt — start by muting/dismissing a typical 'alpha' clip gesture

videoIdeas.title: The general who burned his own ships
videoIdeas.hook: In 711, a commander landed in Spain, looked at his men, and burned every ship they came on. No way back. Here's why that's leadership.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your Tariq bin Ziyad / Andalusia post pulled 437 views — your second best and your only history piece. History storytelling clearly works for your audience. Turn it into a tight leadership lesson instead of a pure history recap.
videoIdeas.script: In 711, a commander landed in Spain, looked at his men, and burned every ship they came on. No retreat. No way back. His name was Tariq bin Ziyad. People remember the fire. They miss the lesson. He didn't burn the ships to be dramatic. He burned them because he understood something about people: given an exit, most will take it the second things get hard. Remove the exit, and they find a strength they didn't know they had. You don't need to burn anything literal. But look at your own life — how many 'ships' are you keeping just in case? The backup plan you feed more than the actual plan. The escape you're quietly rehearsing. Sometimes the most committed thing you can do is cut off your own retreat.

visuals.setting: Storyteller energy — can be talking-head with historical B-roll/maps, or dramatic lighting. Lean into narrative pacing, let the story breathe before the lesson.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text '711 AD' over an image of ships/coast, then cut to you.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open: 'He burned his own ships' with no context, then rewind
On-screen text punchline: 'How many ships are you keeping just in case?'
Dramatic pause and cut on 'No way back'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your top post at 866 views and your best engagement ratio (110 likes, 10 comments). The caption 'Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' is your voice at its best — short, confident, a complete idea in two lines. It's relatable mindset content disguised as a running post, which is why it outperformed everything.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You stumbled into a winning line and then didn't mine it. This single sentence should become a content series on showing up unqualified. Also add one line pointing the metaphor at the viewer ('what room are you avoiding?') to push comments higher — right now people like it but don't have a prompt to respond to.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 437 views and your second-best post — proof your audience wants history told with conviction. The hook 'In 711 AD, Christians were begging Muslims to come and liberate them' is a genuine pattern interrupt that challenges what people assume. This is a clear content lane for you.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments despite strong views means it informed but didn't provoke a response. End history posts with a question or a lesson aimed at the viewer's own life (see the 'burned his own ships' idea). Also the caption got cut mid-sentence — front-load the payoff so the hook survives the 'more' truncation.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 372 views on a throwaay, personal moment ('Never running through a park at night ever again 😭') — proof that short, human, unpolished captions pull their weight. The humour and honesty make you feel like a real person, not an account, which builds the older-brother trust your brand needs.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This is pure personality with no takeaway, so it builds affinity but doesn't establish authority in your three pillars. Keep posting these for texture, but pair the relatability with a point — even one line turning the moment into a mindset observation keeps you on-brand while staying human.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: You tied a universal pain point (burnout) to something concrete (the Sabr app) and opened with 'Burnout affects so many of us, whether you're a medical student or not' — good inclusive hook that widens the audience beyond one niche.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 209 views and only 2 comments — this reads as promotional, and promotional content underperforms your personal content badly. If you're going to feature a product, lead with your own burnout story for the first 10 seconds and introduce the tool late, almost as an afterthought. People engage with your experience, not your endorsement.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — your highest like count anywhere — on a principled, activism post quoting the hadith on changing injustice. This shows your audience rewards moral clarity and courage. When you take a real stance, they show up for it.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 1 comment despite 289 likes — it was a Sidecar (carousel) with no video, and your audience clearly converts best on video. Repackage stances like this as a direct-to-camera video where you say it with your chest. And add a clear call to action (what should they actually do?) so the energy converts into comments and shares, not just silent likes.
